content: 1. Begin the initial inspection of the patient from the foot of the bed. Assess their general appearance, noting any signs of shortness of breath, pain, or other visible distress. Observe their behavior and check for any medical devices or connections, such as IV drips or inhalers, attached to the patient. 2. Use the A VITAMIN C mnemonic for a differential diagnosis checklist. The letters A and C represent Acquired and Congenital conditions, respectively. The remaining letters stand for: Vascular Inflammatory (both infectious and non-infectious) Trauma or Toxins Autoimmune Metabolic Idiopathic Neoplastic For example, when listing causes of decreased vision, consider conditions such as central retinal artery occlusion, retinitis pigmentosa, globe perforation, chronic gentamicin use, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, idiopathic causes, eye tumors, or myopia. 3. When taking a family history, use the BALD CHASM mnemonic to remember key conditions: Blood pressure (hypertension) Arthritis Lung disease Diabetes Cancer Heart disease Alcoholism Stroke Mental health disorders (e.g., depression) 4. Conduct a four-point physical assessment of a disease using the I'm A People Person mnemonic: Inspection Auscultation Percussion Palpation 5. For medical history, use the MJ THREADS mnemonic to cover important diseases: Myocardial infarction Jaundice Tuberculosis Hypertension Rheumatic fever or Rheumatoid arthritis Epilepsy Asthma Diabetes Strokes 6. For past medical history, apply the VAMP THIS mnemonic: Vices (e.g., tobacco, alcohol, drug use, sexual risks) Allergies Medications Preexisting medical conditions Trauma Hospitalizations Immunizations Surgeries 7. Organize the patient examination using the SOAP framework: Subjective: What the patient reports. Objective: What the examiner observes. Assessment: The examiner's interpretation of the findings. Plan: The intended course of action. 8. For the patient profile, use the LADDERS mnemonic: Living situation or Lifestyle Anxiety Depression Daily activities (describe a typical day) Environmental risks or exposures Relationships Support system or Stress 9. When examining lumps or bumps, use the 6 Students and 3 Teachers go for CAMPFIRE mnemonic: Site, Size, Shape, Surface, Skin, Scar Tenderness, Temperature, Transillumination Consistency, Attachment, Mobility, Pulsation, Fluctuation, Irreducibility, Regional lymph nodes, Edge 10. Perform a physical examination in the correct order using the I Palpate People's Abdomens mnemonic: Inspection Palpation Percussion Auscultation 11. For causes of short stature, use the RETARD HEIGHT mnemonic: Rickets Endocrine (e.g., cretinism, hypopituitarism, Cushing's syndrome) Turner syndrome Achondroplasia Respiratory (e.g., suppurative lung disease) Down syndrome Hereditary Environmental (e.g., post-irradiation, post-infectious) Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) Gastrointestinal (e.g., malabsorption) Heart (e.g., congenital heart disease) Tilted backbone (e.g., scoliosis) 12. Differentiate between a sign and a symptom: A sign is something the clinician can detect, even if the patient is unconscious. A symptom is something only the patient can report or describe. 13. Use the INVESTIGATIONS mnemonic as a surgical sieve for diagnostic categories: Iatrogenic Neoplastic Vascular Endocrine Structural or Mechanical Traumatic Inflammatory Genetic or Congenital Autoimmune Toxic Infective Old age or Degenerative Nutritional Spontaneous or Idiopathic 14. For breast history, apply the LMNOP mnemonic: Lump Mammary changes Nipple changes Other symptoms Patient risk factors 15. When delivering bad news, follow the SPIKES protocol: Setting up Perception Invitation Knowledge Emotions Strategy and Summary 16. For common causes of chorea, consider conditions such as Sydenham's chorea, Huntington's disease, or other neurological disorders.
